name: pachi
desc: Software for the Board Game of Go/Weiqi/Baduk
why: A strong open Go engine using Monte Carlo search; a real window into how game AI plays a hard board game.

brief.what_it_is: Pachi is a free, open-source Go (Weiqi/Baduk) playing engine, plus a modular framework for building Go-playing programs. It has no board or user interface of its own. It runs as a GTP client: a Go frontend such as GoGui, Sabaki, or Lizzie sends it moves and time settings over the GTP protocol, and it replies with its own moves. Its default engine uses Monte Carlo tree search and can optionally use a neural network (dcnn) to suggest moves.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes Pachi as both a simple modular framework for Go programs and a reasonably strong engine built on it. The author, Petr Baudis, wrote a master's thesis on its architecture, and the homepage asks users who find it useful in research to cite the Baudis and Gailly paper, 'Pachi: State of the art open source Go program'.
brief.how_it_works: By default it uses a UCT engine that combines Monte Carlo methods with tree search. The tree policy is UCB1AMAF with RAVE, and the semi-random playouts use the 'Moggy' policy, which relies on 3x3 patterns and various tactical checks. MM patterns and deep learning guide the tree search, and the dcnn network is currently used at the root node only.

brief.install_notes: Linux and Windows users can download a binary release from the GitHub releases page. Mac and Linux users can run brew install pachi. Building from source is covered in INSTALL.md. Pachi needs a separate GTP frontend (GoGui recommended, or Sabaki, Lizzie, or kgsGtp for KGS). Neural-network weights come with the release, and other networks are on a 'Pachi Networks' release tag. The default run uses all cores and takes just under 10 seconds per move. Options such as -t, threads=, and max_tree_size= tune this. There is no full options manual; the README points to uct_setoption() in uct/uct.c.
brief.standout: The default engine is a classic MCTS/UCT program with RAVE and hand-built 3x3 playout patterns, not a pure neural-net player. The README says the dcnn adds roughly one stone of strength at large playout counts. The homepage also reports a 7-stone handicap win against 9p Zhou Junxun from a 64-machine cluster, which gives a clear view of how pre-AlphaGo game AI was built.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage says the current stable release is 12.90 (codename Jowa), released Apr 15, 2026. It names lemonsqueeze as the current maintainer and asks for donations to support development. I did not check the last commit date.
brief.caveats: The README warns: 'DO NOT make the GTP interface accessible directly to untrusted users since the parser is not secure.' Pachi has no built-in GUI. The dcnn is used at the root only, and the README says a raw dcnn engine 'won't know when to pass or resign'. --modern-joseki is marked experimental and can leave Pachi unbalanced. The engine options are not comprehensively documented. The homepage says the default engine uses Chinese rules, while the README says Japanese or Chinese. Licence is GPLv2: you can modify and distribute it, but you must release source with any public release. The Autotest framework is MIT.

judge.reason: Pachi offers a hands-on look at classic Go AI: modular UCT search, RAVE, and hand-built playout patterns, rather than just another game interface.

entry.title: Pachi
entry.tldr: An open-source Go engine built on Monte Carlo tree search, showing how game AI played Go before AlphaGo, and it still plays strongly.
entry.deeper_look:
Pachi plays Go (also called Weiqi or Baduk), but it has no board or interface of its own. It speaks GTP, the Go Text Protocol. A frontend such as GoGui, Sabaki or Lizzie sends it moves and time settings, and Pachi replies with its own move. The homepage describes it as "a simple modular framework for programs playing the game of Go/Weiqi/Baduk, and a reasonably strong engine built within this framework."

The default engine is classic Monte Carlo tree search. It plays many semi-random games to the end, using the "Moggy" playout policy, which relies on 3x3 patterns and tactical checks. It then steers the search tree with UCB1AMAF and RAVE statistics. Pattern matching and an optional neural network (dcnn) guide the search, but the network is used at the root node only. The README says the dcnn makes it "about 1 stone stronger" at large playout counts.

The idea underneath is that a game too large to search exhaustively can still be played well by sampling. Pachi shows how that worked before deep-learning players took over. The author, Petr Baudis, wrote a master's thesis on its architecture, and there is a paper, "Pachi: State of the art open source Go program". The homepage also reports a 7-stone handicap win against a 9-dan professional, using a 64-machine cluster.
entry.install:
brew install pachi
# Pachi has no board of its own. You also need a GTP frontend such as GoGui (recommended), Sabaki or Lizzie. kgsGtp is for playing on KGS.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options. The README says there is no full options manual, so this is the starting point.
Lists the neural networks Pachi can use to suggest moves.
Starts the engine with 30 seconds per move on 4 threads and a 500 MB tree cap. It keeps thinking during the opponent's turn. Run it from a GTP frontend.

entry.whats_unique: The default engine is a hand-built MCTS/UCT program with RAVE and pattern-based playouts, not a pure neural-net player. That makes it a readable example of pre-AlphaGo game AI that still plays well.
entry.caveats: It has no GUI and needs a separate GTP frontend. The README warns not to expose its GTP interface to untrusted users because the parser is not secure. Engine options are only documented in the source.
